narrative:
The model estimated an 88% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is a high-risk prediction, not a certainty, but it is strong enough that the admission decision treated you as unlikely to pass and therefore denied your application.

The strongest factor was your third-year class standing: you are in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. This was the largest push toward a failure prediction. The second most influential factor was your LSAT score of 23, well below the accepted-student average of about 37, which also pushed strongly toward failure. Third, your first-year class standing was again the lowest decile, compared with an accepted average near the sixth decile, and it reinforced the same concern. Together, these academic indicators suggested substantially higher bar-exam risk than the typical admitted student.

To improve your chances, focus first on the areas the decision weighed most heavily. Prepare for and retake the LSAT if feasible, and seek academic advising about raising your class standing or addressing the causes of your low first- and third-year ranks. Consider delaying reapplication until you have stronger evidence of readiness, and ask admissions staff what bar-readiness or conditional-admission pathways might be available.
